title: The European Court of Justice
hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.
key_points: The ECJ (Court of Justice of the EU) is the EU's highest court, seated in Luxembourg.
Its job is to interpret EU law so it applies uniformly across all member states.
National courts can refer questions of EU law to it for a binding 'preliminary ruling'.
It can rule that member states or EU institutions have breached EU law — a supranational check on power.
content_html: The European Court of Justice — formally the Court of Justice of the European Union — is the highest court of the EU's legal order, seated in Luxembourg. Unlike a national supreme court, it doesn't sit atop any single country's system; instead it works across borders to make sure European Union law is interpreted and applied the same way in every member state. Without such a court, dozens of national legal systems could read the same EU rule in conflicting ways, and the common rules and single market would fray.
extra_html: Two functions make it powerful. First, when a case in a national court turns on a question of EU law, that court can — and sometimes must — pause and ask the ECJ for a "preliminary ruling," an authoritative answer the national court then applies. Second, the ECJ can hear cases alleging that a member state, or an EU institution itself, has failed to meet its obligations under the treaties. Together these make it a genuinely supranational check: its interpretations bind national courts and governments alike, an arrangement member states accepted when they joined the EU. For students of comparative government it is a leading example of how sovereign states can pool authority and submit to a shared court above the national level — something rare in international relations, where states usually guard the final word for themselves. SCOTUSblog profiles the court for readers more familiar with the U.S. Supreme Court.

related.title: Treaties & International Law
related.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

related.title: The UN & International Organizations
related.hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core job of the European Court of Justice?
flashcards.back_html: To interpret EU law so it is applied uniformly across all member states — it is the EU's highest court, not a replacement for any national supreme court.

flashcards.prompt: What is a 'preliminary ruling' from the ECJ?

choices.text: An authoritative answer on EU law that a national court requests and then applies
A first draft of an EU law before parliament votes on it
A temporary injunction freezing a member state's budget

flashcards.explanation_html: When a case turns on EU law, a national court can refer the question to the ECJ, which gives a binding interpretation the national court applies.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the ECJ a notable example for comparative government?

choices.text: Sovereign states pooled authority and submitted to a shared court above the national level
It is controlled by whichever member state is largest
It can only issue non-binding advisory opinions

flashcards.explanation_html: Member states accepted a supranational court whose rulings bind national courts and governments alike — rare among sovereign nations that usually guard their final say.
